summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Indonesia's institutional posture toward LGBT people has an identifiable starting point. An August 2016 Human Rights Watch report recorded that the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities mental illnesses and recommended psychological rehabilitation, while the Jokowi government remained mostly silent. Human Rights Watch has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016.

Abuse has extended into education. A July 2026 Human Rights Watch briefing described a surge in abuse against LGBT students following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia, with the LGBT umbrella organisation Arus Pelangi documenting 94 cases. In early July 2026 officials called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

The October 2025 presidential decree did not create the violence so much as supply doctrine for it: analysis published in August 2026 links the attacks on trans women to officials' verbal attacks and to the decree's treatment of LGBT people as risks to be monitored and controlled under national defence policy.

Censorship machinery is broader than the penal code. Beyond the pornography statute and the 2016 broadcasting ban, the government shut down the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni and, in 2025, was discussing a new bill to explicitly prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour.

Regional comparison: Aceh stands apart as the province where Sharia provisions are publicly enforced by caning, while national-level morality provisions and provincial criminalisation in South Sumatra operate through conventional courts and police action.
localsOnly:
Transgender Indonesians can change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they may marry someone of the opposite legal gender.

Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identity papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua. Many were undocumented, especially where families disapproved, leaving them without access to work or social services. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised; transgender Indonesians have their gender at birth printed unless they have already obtained court recognition.

Since 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) 'socially dysfunctional', regularly conducted raids against them, and taken detained trans individuals to city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres where they are incarcerated alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their 'offence'; officials stated the measure is meant as a deterrent against being transgender.

Conversion therapy is widely practiced and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, including corrective rape by family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on safe houses and evacuation plans. Yayasan Srikandi Sejati provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, and Yogyakarta has the only madrasa for transgender people in the world.

As of 2019 no specific law protects Indonesian citizens from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Theoretically, protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground is guaranteed in the Constitution and Human Rights Law No. 39/1999. The Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer declaring LGBTQ persons need not apply after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights.

A police brigadier, identified as TT, was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him; his lawsuit was rejected by the Semarang State Administrative Court in May 2019 on procedural grounds. The police have issued a circular since 2015 to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and Regulation of the Head of National Police Number 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses Indonesian entry and visa screening, airport questioning of trans travellers, or how Indonesian consulates assess marker mismatches on foreign passports. Those questions remain unresolved for this record.

Whether a foreign visitor carrying an X or otherwise incongruent passport descriptor would be refused document processing or entry is not sourced here.

Enforcement frequency under the 2026 penal code is described only as selective; no case count, charging data or sentence data for consensual same-sex relations since 2 January 2026 appears in the inventory.

Whether South Sumatra's provincial criminalisation provisions have been enforced against foreigners, and how often Aceh's caning sentences are imposed on visitors rather than residents, is not sourced.

The 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour is described as under discussion; its enactment status at the time of writing is unresolved.

Deaths in custody of trans detainees other than the 2022 Bali case, and any official inquiry outcome in that case, are not covered by the sources gathered here.
